title: CAP theorem
description: Understand the CAP theorem and its implications for distributed system design. Learn to make informed trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

data.text: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can only provide two out of three guarantees: **Consistency**, **Availability**, and **Partition Tolerance**. When a network partition occurs, you must choose between consistency and availability.
Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.

items: Linearizability—operations appear atomic and instantaneous
Strong consistency—no stale reads allowed
Requires coordination between nodes
Often implemented via quorum-based replication

data.text: Every request receives a (non-error) response, without the guarantee that it contains the most recent write.

items: System remains responsive during failures
No requests block or timeout indefinitely
May return stale or outdated data
Prioritizes uptime over data freshness

data.text: The system continues to operate despite arbitrary message loss or failure of part of the system.

items: Network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems
System must function when communication between nodes fails
In practice, P is non-negotiable for distributed systems
The real choice is between C and A when P occurs

data.title: Key Insight
data.text: In distributed systems, network partitions will happen. You can't avoid P, so you must choose between C and A when a partition occurs.

items.title: CP Systems (Consistency + Partition Tolerance)
items.description: Choose consistency over availability. During a partition, the system may reject writes or block reads to avoid inconsistency. Examples: HBase, MongoDB, Redis with strong consistency.

items.title: AP Systems (Availability + Partition Tolerance)
items.description: Choose availability over consistency. During a partition, the system continues serving requests, possibly with stale data. Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB.

data.text: The choice depends on your application's requirements and the cost of inconsistency versus downtime.

items: Choose CP for financial systems, inventory management, any system where wrong data is unacceptable
Choose AP for social media feeds, caching layers, analytics, any system where stale data is tolerable
Many systems offer tunable consistency—let you choose per-operation
Consider your business requirements: can you afford to show wrong data, or can you afford to be unavailable?
CAP is not about normal operation—it's about behavior during partitions
You can have all three in single-node systems, but not in distributed systems
CAP doesn't mean you can't have eventual consistency in AP systems
The theorem describes a trade-off, not a strict binary choice in practice

data.title: Beyond CAP
data.text: The PACELC theorem extends CAP by adding latency considerations. When there's no partition, you trade off between consistency and latency.
